extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, political communicators, and scholars of public opinion and mass media
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting messages, stories, and images that enlist popular interest in public affairs — how to make political/press/artistic material engaging and comprehensible to mass audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize and dramatize abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: We tend to personalize quantities, and to dramatize relations. Social Movements, Economic Forces, National Interests, Public Opinion are treated as persons, or persons like the Pope, the President ... become ideas and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use allegory and personification so abstract social, economic, or political phenomena are experienced as human actions and relationships; this makes complex matters more economical and memorable. Beware oversimplification, but recognize that most audiences need an identifiable human dimension to grasp public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear handles for identification (mark the hero/villain)
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular representation the handles for identification are almost always marked. You know who the hero is at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters, roles, or sides instantly recognizable so audiences can quickly locate someone to identify with; unclear marking reduces popular appeal. Strong, visible cues (symbols, behavior, roles) speed identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the audience something to do (active engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must have something to do, and the contemplation of the true, the good and the beautiful is not something to do. ... the audience must be exercised by the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narratives and images that invite participation (taking sides, imagining acting as the hero) rather than passive aesthetic contemplation. Engagement is achieved by conflict, stakes, and opportunities for vicarious action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use powerful, arousing motifs (sexual passion and fighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forms of exercise which far transcend all others ... They are sexual passion and fighting, and the two have so many associations with each other ... that a fight about sex outranks every other theme in the breadth of its appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ motifs that readily arouse broad interest — especially struggle/combative conflict and sexuality — knowing these have cross-cultural, cross-class appeal. Note: sexual motifs are less used in American political imagery, but fighting/issue motifs are ubiquitous and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicit suspense via struggle (antagonist, obstacle, problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plot lacks suspense: 1. Add an antagonist, 2. Add an obstacle, 3. Add a problem, 4. Emphasize one of the questions in the picture ... the element of struggle, which never fails to arouse suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create or foreground conflict and unresolved questions to hold attention; practical tactics include introducing an antagonist, clear obstacles, and emphasizing unresolved stakes. Suspense transforms attention into sustained involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic beginning, romantic (desirable) ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Our popular taste is to have the drama originate in a setting realistic enough to make identification plausible and to have it terminate in a setting romantic enough to be desirable, but not so romantic as to be inconceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor stories in believable detail to permit identification, then move toward an optimistic, emotionally satisfying resolution — but avoid wholly implausible fantasy or relentless realism that ends in defeat. Balance familiarity and aspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization: use pictures and imagery to make ideas real
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures have always been the surest way of conveying an idea, and next in order, words that call up pictures in memory. ... no idea is lucid for practical decision until it has visual or tactile value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate abstract claims into concrete visual or tactile images; use descriptive language, photographs, scenes, or metaphors that audiences can 'see' and thus more readily internalize and act upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of allegory and reliance on stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: The bewildering variety of our impressions ... tends to force us to adopt the greater economy of the allegory. The deepest of all the stereotypes is the human stereotype which imputes human nature to inanimate or collective things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on shared allegories and stereotypes to compress complex information into familiar, quickly grasped forms. Recognize that stereotypes simplify and shape perception; they are efficient but risk distortion and entrenchment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align with prevailing stereotypes for commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: The men who make moving pictures ... must adhere to the stereotypes that they find, or pay the price of frustrating expectation. The stereotypes can be altered; but not in time to guarantee success when the film is released six months from now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resources and timelines demand mass appeal, conform to current audience expectations and stereotypes; innovation is possible but risky and often not commercially feasible in the short term. Pioneers who alter stereotypes accept commercial penalties but may be rewarded in other ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda/message formula: plausible analysis, avoid tedium, then promise heaven
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilful propagandist knows that while you must start with a plausible analysis, you must not keep on analyzing, because the tedium of real political accomplishment will soon destroy interest. So the propagandist exhausts the interest in reality by a tolerably plausible banning, and then stokes up energy for a long voyage by brandishing a passport to heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a believable depiction of present problems to gain credibility, but shift away from dry detailed analysis before it bores the audience; instead supply a clear, hopeful vision or promised outcome to sustain energy and commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enmesh public fiction with private urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula works when the public fiction enmeshes itself with a private urgency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link public narratives to private concerns and emotions so that collective stories feel personally relevant. Messages that connect with individuals' immediate wants, fears, or identities convert abstract issues into motivating forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messaging to the specific 'self' engaged
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no one self always at work. ... it is of great importance in the formation of any public opinion, what self is engaged. ... it makes a whole lot of difference whether you conceive the demand as a desire to grow fruit or to marry the white man's daughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by which identity/self is salient (economic actor, parent, patriot, moral agent, etc.) and frame messages to address that self's concerns and modes of judgment; the same factual claim will be received differently depending on which self is invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for audience heterogeneity and abstraction needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequently the more mixed the audience, the greater will be the variation in the response. ... As the audience grows larger, the number of common words diminishes. Thus the common factors in the story become more abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing broad, diverse publics, use more abstract, widely shared symbols and themes rather than detailed, idiosyncratic particulars. Expect reinterpretation across subgroups and design core messages that survive varied re-readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect stories to be reinterpreted by each listener
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore, the identical story is not the same story to all who hear it. Each will enter it at a slightly different point, since no two experiences are exactly alike; he will reenact it in his own way, and transfuse it with his own feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that audiences will personalize, stress, twist, and embroider stories; craft core elements that are robust to such reworking and consider how rumors or retellings will alter reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare characters/people for likely situations (role education)
rubrics_metrics.description: The preparation of characters for all the situations in which men may find themselves is one function of a moral education. Clearly then, it depends for its success upon the sincerity and knowledge with which the environment has been explored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long-term social outcomes, cultivate norms, roles, and 'characters' through education and culture so people have repertoires of appropriate responses in varied circumstances. Message design should consider whether audiences have internalized the roles needed to act on the message.
